prompt: In Cicero's story, how did Simonides tell the crushed guests apart?
options: He remembered the place where each one had sat
He recognised their rings and clothing
He had written the guest list down
The two young men at the gate told him
correctAnswer: He remembered the place where each one had sat
explanation: The bodies were too crushed to recognise, but Simonides recalled the place in which each guest had sat. Order in space did the remembering.

prompt: Drill recall: the fourth thing you placed on your first walk through your home was a _____.
correctAnswer: trumpet
explanation: The six were a goldfish, a ladder, a birthday cake, a trumpet, a snowman and an umbrella. If it did not come back, stand in place 4 and make the trumpet louder.

prompt: It is an established historical fact that Simonides invented the memory palace on the day a banquet hall collapsed.
correctAnswer: False
explanation: This is the myth. Cicero tells it as something people say, about four centuries after the poet died, and Quintilian found his authorities disagreeing about the details and called the Castor and Pollux part purely fictitious. It is a founding legend.

prompt: What lesson does Cicero draw from the Simonides story?
options: Faces are easier to remember than places
It is chiefly order that gives distinctness to memory
Poets have better memories than orators
Memory works best when you repeat a list aloud
correctAnswer: It is chiefly order that gives distinctness to memory
explanation: Simonides is said to have discovered that order is the key: fix a series of places, set images in them, and the order of the places preserves the order of the things.

prompt: Match each part of the method to Cicero's comparison or role:

pairs.right: Credited by legend with the method

explanation: Cicero says to use the places like a wax tablet and the images like letters, so that the order of the places preserves the order of the things. Simonides gets the credit in the legend.

prompt: You are choosing your very first memory palace. Which is the best choice?
options: A famous palace you once saw in a film
A different random building every time
A list of room names written on a card
Your own home, walked in your usual order
correctAnswer: Your own home, walked in your usual order
explanation: Home is ideal because you already know its order without effort. A building you barely know, or one that keeps changing, means memorising the palace as well as the list.

prompt: Drill recall: put the six things from your first walk in the order you placed them.
explanation: Walk the route from the front door: goldfish, ladder, birthday cake, trumpet, snowman, umbrella. The places kept the order for you.

prompt: Which step of this retelling of the legend is wrong?
steps: Simonides recites a poem at a feast given by Scopas
Scopas pays only half the fee and tells him to ask Castor and Pollux for the rest
Simonides is called outside to meet two young men and finds nobody
Simonides is trapped under the rubble and guesses the guests' names at random
The families cannot recognise the bodies, so Simonides names them by where they sat
explanation: Simonides was outside when the hall fell in, and he did not guess: he remembered where each guest had sat. That is the whole point of the story.

prompt: The Ad Herennium says your places should be in a busy, crowded spot so the images feel lively.
correctAnswer: False
explanation: The opposite: choose a deserted rather than a crowded region, because people passing to and fro blur the images while solitude keeps their outlines sharp.

prompt: In the Ad Herennium, what goes in the fifth place so that you never lose count?
options: A friend called Decimus
A burning candle
A wax tablet
A golden hand
correctAnswer: A golden hand
explanation: A golden hand marks the fifth place and a friend whose first name is Decimus marks the tenth; then every fifth place after that gets a mark too.

prompt: Your palace is a corridor of eight identical office doors, and you keep forgetting which door held which image. What does the handbook say to change?
options: Add more identical doors
Walk the corridor faster
Choose places that differ in form and nature
Make the corridor brighter
correctAnswer: Choose places that differ in form and nature
explanation: The handbook warns that many look-alike places, like a run of identical spaces between columns, leave you unsure what you put in each. Distinct places keep images from swapping homes.

prompt: Match each faulty place to the problem the Ad Herennium warns about:

pairs.right: You forget what is in each

explanation: Each rule prevents a specific failure: moderate size, moderate light, solitude and distinct places all keep each image sharp and in its own home.

prompt: A friend insists a memory palace must be a huge, real building you know intimately. What does the evidence say?
options: Moderate places work best, and a briefly studied virtual place worked as well as a familiar one for beginners
Only real palaces work, as the name suggests
The bigger the building, the better the recall
Imaginary places never work
correctAnswer: Moderate places work best, and a briefly studied virtual place worked as well as a familiar one for beginners
explanation: This is the myth. The handbook wants places of moderate size and says imagination can build settings when real ones run short; Legge and colleagues found briefly studied virtual environments as effective as familiar ones for novices.

prompt: The Ad Herennium compares the places to wax tablets and the images to _____.
correctAnswer: letters
explanation: Places are the tablet, images the letters, their arrangement the script and delivery the reading. The tablet stays while the letters can be wiped and rewritten.

prompt: Which of these rules for places is NOT from the Ad Herennium?
steps: Choose a deserted rather than a crowded region
Make the places differ in form and nature
Make every place as bright as possible, so the images glitter
Space them moderately, about thirty feet apart
explanation: The handbook wants places neither too bright nor too dim, so that shadows do not hide the images and glare does not make them glitter.

prompt: Why does the Ad Herennium insist that the places form a series, with every fifth one marked?
options: So that the palace looks grander
So the order is never lost or miscounted, whichever way you walk
Because Romans could only count in fives
So that two images can share each place
correctAnswer: So the order is never lost or miscounted, whichever way you walk
explanation: A fixed series lets you go forwards or backwards from any place without confusion, and the marks at five and ten tell you instantly if you have skipped a place.

prompt: Drill recall: the seventh item on your shopping list was _____.
correctAnswer: lemons
explanation: The list ran eggs, toothpaste, bananas, lightbulbs, teabags, wrapping paper, lemons, batteries, cheese, bin bags. Two places after the golden hand: lemons.

prompt: Once a palace has been filled with one list, it cannot be reused for another.
correctAnswer: False
explanation: This is the myth. The Ad Herennium says images fade with disuse while the places abide, and Massen and Vaterrodt-Plünnecke found interference was no worse for the method of loci than for other methods. Rotating routes helps further.

prompt: Drill recall: reading your shopping list backwards from the tenth place, the third item you meet is _____.
correctAnswer: batteries
explanation: Backwards from Decimus: bin bags, cheese, batteries. A series works in either direction, just as the Ad Herennium promised.

prompt: You are recalling a list and place 6 seems empty. What should you do?
options: Repeat the whole list aloud ten times
Stand in place 6 in your mind, look for the faint image, strengthen it and walk on
Start again from the front door
Abandon the rest of the palace
correctAnswer: Stand in place 6 in your mind, look for the faint image, strengthen it and walk on
explanation: The place itself is still there, which tells you where the gap is. Look for the faint image, make it louder, and carry on; there is no need to restart.

prompt: What did Twomey and Kroneisen's 2021 meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials conclude?
options: A medium effect in favour of the method, though many trials carried a high risk of bias
The method has no effect at all
A huge effect with no weaknesses in the evidence
The method only works for memory champions
correctAnswer: A medium effect in favour of the method, though many trials carried a high risk of bias
explanation: They found an effect size of 0.65, robust to adjustments for publication bias, but most trials did not report how they randomised people. Good initial support, not the last word.

prompt: Match each source to what it says about reusing places:

pairs.right: Images fade with disuse; places abide
Interference no worse for loci than other methods
About 70% recall of a high-interference list

explanation: Ancient advice and modern tests agree that palaces can be reused, especially if you rotate several routes.

prompt: Yesterday you put a list of fruits in your home palace. Today you need to memorise a different list of fruits. What is the best plan?
options: Give up the method for similar lists
Put two fruits in every place
Use a different route today and let yesterday's images fade
Use the same route: interference never happens
correctAnswer: Use a different route today and let yesterday's images fade
explanation: Interference appeared when lists came from the same category, and Dresler's training plans rotated routes to reduce interference from earlier lists. A different route sidesteps the problem.

prompt: Drill recall: put these items from your shopping list in palace order.
explanation: They sat in places 2, 4, 5, 6, 8 and 10. The teabags were on the golden hand and the bin bags on Decimus.

prompt: How many of the ten superior memorisers in Maguire's 2003 study used the method of loci?
options: Nine
Two
Five
None: they relied on natural talent
correctAnswer: Nine
explanation: All ten used mnemonics, and nine of the ten used the method of loci for some or all of the tasks.

prompt: Drill recall: the fifth word on your outdoor route, sitting on the golden hand, was _____.
correctAnswer: pearl
explanation: The route ran anchor, violin, cactus, helmet, pearl, kettle, rocket, scarf, lighthouse, tortoise.

prompt: Maguire's team found that memory champions have structurally different brains and exceptional intellect.
correctAnswer: False
explanation: This is the myth. Superior memory was not driven by exceptional intellectual ability or structural brain differences; what differed was the strategy and the brain activity it produced.

prompt: Which regions did the champions engage more than the controls while learning?
options: None: their brain activity matched the controls exactly
Medial parietal cortex, retrosplenial cortex and right posterior hippocampus
Visual cortex, cerebellum and brainstem
Broca's area, Wernicke's area and the amygdala
correctAnswer: Medial parietal cortex, retrosplenial cortex and right posterior hippocampus
explanation: These three regions are important for memory and implicated in spatial memory and navigation, which fits a strategy built on walking through places.

prompt: You test a memory champion against an untrained friend. On which material would you expect the champion's lead to be smallest?
options: Snowflake pictures that are hard to put into words
Three-digit numbers
Faces
All three: the lead is the same for every material
correctAnswer: Snowflake pictures that are hard to put into words
explanation: The gap was greatest for three-digit numbers, then faces, and smallest for snowflakes. A palace needs images you can name or picture.

prompt: Drill recall: put these words from your outdoor route in the order you placed them.
explanation: They sat in places 2, 4, 6, 7, 9 and 10 of your outdoor route.

prompt: Which step in this summary of Maguire's 2003 study is wrong?
steps: Ten superior memorisers, mostly top World Memory Championships competitors, were compared with matched volunteers
Standard tests showed no exceptional intellectual ability
Structural scans showed the champions had unusually large hippocampi
Functional scans showed extra activity in regions tied to spatial memory
Nine of the ten used the method of loci
explanation: The structural scans found no brain differences. The difference was in what the brain did during learning, not in its shape.

prompt: Why did Maguire's team call for a study of people newly taught the method of loci?
options: To prove that the champions were born different
Their results could reflect years of practice or a special flair for the method, and novices could separate the two
The champions refused to be scanned again
Nobody had tried the method before 2003
correctAnswer: Their results could reflect years of practice or a special flair for the method, and novices could separate the two
explanation: The champions had practised for more than eleven years on average, so the team could not tell practice from talent. Training novices, as Dresler's team later did, tests it directly.

prompt: In Dresler's 2017 study, how much did the method-of-loci group train?
options: Six weeks: 40 sessions of 30 minutes
One afternoon
A year of daily practice
Six months, an hour a day
correctAnswer: Six weeks: 40 sessions of 30 minutes
explanation: The trainees practised 30 minutes a day for 40 days at home, after a two-hour introductory course.

prompt: Memory palace training has been shown to prevent dementia.
correctAnswer: False
explanation: This is the myth. None of these studies tested it: Dresler's trainees were young men learning word lists, and Maguire's team wrote that the value of mnemonics in brain injury and disease is less clear. The method is not a treatment or a prevention.

prompt: After six weeks of loci training, Dresler's novices went from recalling an average of 26 words out of 72 to about _____.
explanation: They more than doubled their recall, and the advantage persisted at the four-month follow-up.

prompt: A friend says any hard brain workout, like the n-back game, boosts word recall as much as a memory palace. What did Dresler's study find?
options: Nobody improved
The loci group improved significantly more, and the n-back and no-training groups did not differ
The n-back group improved the most
All three groups improved equally
correctAnswer: The loci group improved significantly more, and the n-back and no-training groups did not differ
explanation: This is the myth. The benefit came from the method of loci itself, not from effortful mental exercise in general.

prompt: Drill recall: the tenth word you placed in your twelve-place palace was _____.
correctAnswer: jealousy
explanation: The twelve were volcano, freedom, umbrella, piano, honesty, penguin, thunder, history, cushion, jealousy, bicycle, silence. Decimus held jealousy.

prompt: Match each study to its finding:

pairs.right: Novices from 26 to 62 words in six weeks
Less brain activity during learning after training

explanation: Together they say the method works, can be learned in weeks, and changes how the brain does the job rather than its structure.

prompt: Drill recall: put these words from your twelve-place palace in order.
explanation: They sat in places 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9 and 12. Honesty was on the golden hand.

prompt: Which conclusion goes beyond what Dresler's study showed?
options: Trainees' brain connectivity shifted towards the athletes' patterns
Six weeks of loci training will protect any adult against dementia
Loci training improved word-list recall in young men
The gains were still present four months later
correctAnswer: Six weeks of loci training will protect any adult against dementia
explanation: The study tested young men on word lists. It said nothing about dementia, and the method should never be treated as medicine.
